lines: Quick question. Where were you, mentally, five seconds ago?
If you are like most people, not entirely here.
In a famous study, researchers used a smartphone app to ask thousands of people, at random moments, what they were doing and what they were thinking about.
Their minds were somewhere else nearly half the time. The average mind is a tourist who rarely stays at its own address.
This is the third film in a small series. The first was about the past. The second was about the future.
This one is about the only place where experience actually happens.
In the fourth century, Saint Augustine noticed something odd about time.
He wrote that there are really three presents. The present of things past, which is memory. The present of things present, which is attention. And the present of things future, which is expectation.
Every memory you have ever had was experienced now. Every plan you have ever made was made now.
The first two films were about two of those presents. The past, rebuilt in the present. The future, imagined in the present.
Which leaves the one that holds all the others.
But what is the present, exactly?
It is not a point. Psychologists, starting with William James, describe the experienced present as a short window, a few seconds wide, in which things feel like they are happening together.
And it is built. Signals from your eyes and ears take time to be processed, so what you experience as now is assembled a fraction of a second after the world did it.
Your brain smooths over the delay by predicting what comes next, and stitching it together.
You are watching live television, with a slight delay and an extremely good editor.
Which means your sense of now is not a window onto reality. It is a very skilled reconstruction. One that you get to steer, a little, with attention.
James had another line worth keeping. My experience, he wrote, is what I agree to attend to.
In nineteen ninety nine, Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris asked people to count basketball passes in a video.
Midway through, a person in a gorilla suit walks into the middle of the court, faces the camera, thumps their chest, and leaves.
About half of the viewers never saw it.
This is called inattentional blindness. It is not stupidity. It is what attention does. It is a spotlight, and the world outside it goes quiet.
Which is both a little alarming and strangely hopeful. If attention builds your experience, then where you put it matters.
Now a brilliant, slightly annoying experiment by Daniel Kahneman and colleagues.

People put one hand in painfully cold water for sixty seconds. In another trial, they put the other hand in for sixty seconds, followed by thirty more seconds in water that was slightly warmer, still unpleasant.
Offered a choice of which trial to repeat, most people chose the longer one. The one with more total pain.
Because memory is a poor accountant. It keeps the worst moment and the ending, and mostly ignores how long things lasted.
Kahneman described two points of view: the experiencing self and the remembering self. One lives your life. The other writes the review.
The review matters. But the life is what is happening right now, and no one has written that review yet.
Meanwhile, many of us find it surprisingly hard to just be here.
In a set of eleven studies, Timothy Wilson and colleagues left people alone in a room with nothing to do but think, for six to fifteen minutes.
Most did not enjoy it. And many preferred to give themselves mild electric shocks rather than sit with their thoughts.
Critics have argued that the results were overstated, and that thinking is not always unpleasant. Both can be true. Quiet can feel strange when you are not used to it.
Humans: the species that can be bored in an empty room, and then reach for a shock button.
If that is you, you are in very good company. It is most of us.
Back to the wandering mind. In that smartphone study, people reported being less happy when their minds wandered than when they were focused on what they were doing.
But later studies add a kind and important detail. What matters a great deal is what the wandering thoughts are like. Interesting, pleasant wandering has been linked with a good mood.
So the goal is not to stop your mind from wandering. That would be like asking the ocean to stop having waves.
The goal is to notice where you are. Then you get to choose.
And remember, the wandering is just your memory machine and your future machine doing what they do best, in the background of your life.
What actually helps? Mindfulness is the most studied approach, so let us be honest about what the evidence says.

A large review in JAMA Internal Medicine pooled forty seven trials. It found moderate evidence that mindfulness programs reduce anxiety, depression, and pain, with small to moderate effects, and no evidence that they beat other active treatments.
A later analysis of individual data from fifteen trials found a small to moderate reduction in distress among community adults, regardless of age or gender.
So, not magic. But real, modest, and free.
Meditation is not about becoming a calm statue. It is about noticing, again and again, that you wandered, and coming back without giving yourself a lecture.
The coming back is the whole exercise. Every time you notice, you have done one repetition.
There is another door into the present, and it is delightfully cheap. It is awe.

In experiments led by Melanie Rudd, people who felt awe, compared with other emotions, reported feeling that they had more time available, and were less impatient. They were also more willing to volunteer their time to help others.
The researchers suggested that awe pulls people into the present moment, and that this is what changes how time feels.
So a minute under a big sky, or beside a river, or really looking at the face of someone you love, is not wasted time. It may be the opposite.
It is also much cheaper than a vacation, and you do not have to pack.
So what is the true nature of experience? Science cannot answer the deepest version of that question, and anyone who says otherwise is selling something.
But it does tell us three things we can use.
Experience is always happening now. The past and the future are things you do now.
Experience is constructed. Your brain assembles it from prediction, memory, and attention.
And experience is steerable. A little. Gently. Through where you place your attention, and how kindly you hold whatever arrives.
The philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein wrote that if eternity means timelessness rather than endless time, then eternal life belongs to those who live in the present.
So here is a very small invitation.
Take one slow breath. Feel the air, and the chair, and the sound of whatever is nearby.
That is it. That is the whole present. It has been here the whole time, waiting politely.
The past is a story you are telling now. The future is a story you are telling now. And this, right here, is where you get to be kind.
You may now return to your regularly scheduled wandering.
Thank you for watching.
The studies mentioned in this film are listed on screen.
